analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off most of the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: referred to a House subcommittee in March 1999, it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from selling or issuing new oil and gas leases within roughly 50 to 175 miles of the coast in every Atlantic, Pacific, and eastern Gulf-adjacent state from Florida to Washington, while leaving the Central and Western Gulf of Mexico open to drilling [S2] [S3]. Existing leases would have been honored until they expired, and a handful of already-leased areas off Florida would have been canceled with the leaseholders compensated, potentially through credits on federal royalties from other leases [S3]. The bill was sent to the House Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, where it sat without action until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents and the businesses that depend on clean water — fishing, tourism, and beach economies along the Atlantic, Pacific, and Florida coasts — would gain permanent protection from new offshore drilling near their shores. Taxpayers would also avoid paying compensation to a small set of Florida leaseholders only in the narrow sense that the buyout never happened, but the bill itself would have spent public money to cancel those leases [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease, permit, or license for oil or gas exploration or extraction on submerged lands within 50 to 175 miles of the coast of every Atlantic and Pacific coastal state, including areas previously covered by moratoriums [S3].
Permanently ends drilling access in those waters after any existing lease expires, rather than leaving the decision to each year's appropriations process [S3].
Directs the Interior Secretary to report within nine months on options for compensating leaseholders of two dozen Florida blocks, including royalty credits, to retire those leases [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies would lose access to new drilling territory off the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and the federal government (and ultimately taxpayers) would bear the cost of compensating holders of canceled Florida leases, potentially by forgoing royalty revenue on other federal leases [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore drillers and federal royalty revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill would require the government to cancel certain existing Florida leases and pay the leaseholders compensation under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, with options including credits against federal royalties — a real cost to taxpayers and federal revenue [S3].

By excluding the Central and Western Gulf of Mexico, the bill concentrates future drilling in the Gulf rather than reducing national oil and gas dependence, and it would keep potential domestic energy resources off limits [S2] [S3].

The bill drew only four cosponsors and no committee action, so it offered no evidence of the broader support that would have been needed to overcome the Resources Committee's control over offshore energy policy [S4] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For coastal states, the benefit is durable protection of fisheries, beaches, and tourism from new drilling, with the main cost being compensation owed to a limited set of Florida leaseholders and forgone federal leasing revenue. The carve-out for the Central and Western Gulf means the bill shifts drilling rather than eliminating it, which is a fair criticism but not a fatal flaw for coastal communities it protects.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank LoBiondo introduced the bill on February 25, 1999, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Resources [S1] [S5].
On March 10, 1999, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, with executive comment requested from the Interior Department — the last action of any kind recorded [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill expired when the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas companies kept the door open to future Atlantic and Pacific leasing, and Florida leaseholders avoided being bought out of their leases. Coastal communities did not gain the permanent drilling ban the bill offered. Oil and gas companies and their leaseholders came out ahead

for.name: Rep. Frank A. LoBiondo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban new offshore oil and gas leasing off the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.

for.name: 4 Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no further recorded action.

against.name: House Committee on Resources
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over offshore energy leasing
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on March 10, 1999, and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans, but the record shows no votes or floor debate, so the partisan shape of broader support cannot be measured [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have closed off new leasing across most of the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, ending industry access to that territory after existing leases expire. Its death left that access open, though annual moratoriums in place at the time continued to restrict much of the same area [S3].

A permanent drilling ban would have protected the beaches, fisheries, and water quality these industries depend on from spills and rig construction near shore. They gained nothing because the bill died [S3].

The bill would have canceled a set of existing leases off Florida and required compensation, potentially via royalty credits — a payout to the leaseholders funded by federal royalty revenue. Because the bill died, these leaseholders kept their leases outright instead.
